analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 1999 and died when the 106th Congress ended, drawing zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have erased the federal taxes owed when someone dies or gives away large amounts of wealth, including the tax on transfers that skip a generation. The estate tax only applies to very large fortunes, so the entire benefit would go to the wealthiest families. The bill was introduced by Senator Allard with no cosponsors, sent to the Finance Committee, and never moved again [S1] [S2] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Families with the largest estates. Only estates above a substantial exemption threshold owed any estate tax, and the biggest fortunes paid the most, so repeal would have functioned as a large tax cut concentrated at the very top of the wealth distribution. Heirs to large businesses and investment portfolios would have kept those assets intact instead of paying tax on the transfer.

how_it_helps.text: Wipes out the estate and gift taxes entirely, so no estate above any size would owe federal transfer tax after enactment [S2] [S3].

Also repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which targets wealth passed directly to grandchildren to evade a generation of estate tax, a provision that matters only for very large fortunes [S2] [S3].
The repeal would apply to deaths and gifts after enactment, so estates currently in planning would immediately escape the tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax was a progressive tax paid almost entirely by the largest estates; removing it would have shifted the burden of funding the government onto everyone else through other taxes, larger deficits, or reduced spending.

drawbacks.text: The benefit is concentrated entirely among the wealthiest families, since the estate tax only applies to large estates, making this a top-heavy tax cut [S2].
Repeal would permanently remove a major source of federal revenue that is borne by those best able to pay, leaving the cost to be made up by other taxpayers or debt [S2].
The bill contains no replacement revenue or offset of any kind; it simply repeals subtitle B of the tax code [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a large, permanent tax cut for a small number of very wealthy families, paid for by everyone else through lost federal revenue with no offset. The estate tax touches only a small fraction of estates, so for the vast majority of Americans the direct benefit is zero and the indirect cost is real. The bill also skipped the usual debate over revenue replacement entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Allard introduced the bill on July 1, 1999, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1] [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and the full action history shows nothing after the referral to committee [S5].
The bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off that the bill died, because the federal estate tax — paid almost exclusively by the largest estates — remained in place and continued to fund the government progressively. The wealth of the largest fortunes would have passed untaxed had it passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers, who kept the estate tax

for.name: Sen. Wayne Allard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote and no other senator signed on, so no record shows where the parties stood; the bill simply drew no support beyond its sponsor [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Had the bill passed, heirs to the largest fortunes would have saved the entire estate tax bill on their inheritance. It died, so those families kept paying the tax that applies only to estates above a high threshold.

industries.industry: Estate planning professionals (lawyers, wealth advisers, trust companies)
industries.note: Repeal would have eliminated the need for much estate-tax planning, costing the wealth-planning industry business. Its loss would have come alongside a revenue cost to the public, so the alignment is incidental.
The estate tax is a progressive revenue source paid by the largest estates; repeal with no offset would have shifted the funding burden onto everyone else.
